voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
Jesus is our Lord, the crucified one we met in the poor and kept at the hours. At Tours, Martin, alone in his cell, refused a devil dressed as a crowned Christ: Sulpitius reports Martin telling a devil disguised as a crowned Christ that he would believe only in a Christ showing the wounds of the cross: “The Lord Jesus never said he would come back dressed in purple, with a glittering crown on his head. I will not believe Christ has come unless he comes looking the way he did when he suffered, and openly shows the marks of his wounds from the cross.”

Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught the same meeting in a different form. At the sixth hour we kept what Cassian handed us from Palestine and Mesopotamia: the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father, went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world, and took away the debt that could not be paid. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell; no one took his life from him, he laid it down himself and took it again. And the good news as we told it: he calls us to himself while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.

glosses.plain_meaning: The monk's own dwelling, and the place where everything happens to him. There Martin prays, receives saints, and is tempted by a purple-robed devil behind a closed door. There Cassian's junior may not go out without leave, stays all day at his work, and is assailed at noon by the disease that makes him hate the cell itself.
glosses.quick_meaning: The monk's own hut or cave, rarely left except for prayer - where saints and the devil come, and where the wandering heart is held still.
glosses.translational_sense: 'A cell - like a prison, or a private room?' - neither: it is the one place a monk is, a wooden hut or a hollow in the rock he rarely leaves except for prayer, where saints and the devil appear, and in the south a harbour whose barriers hold the wandering heart still by labour and rule - with its own named affliction at noon.

confidence.divergence_note: Documented as to existence, office, and reputation: Sulpitius's Life, Letters, Dialogues, and Sacred History within or just after Martin's own lifetime, corroborated independently by Gennadius ch. XIX (ancient text: "monk and bishop," "a man famous for signs and wonders and virtues"). Everything narrated of him rests on one author, so every story is Widely Accepted, never Documented, at the narrative level (Doc_01 §2.2's rule that one ancient witness is not multiple independent sources); the two stories whose narrative claim is the wonder itself are Tier 3. The year of his birth, of the cloak, of the discharge, and of the election are not given in the text (the emperor is "Julian Caesar," the monastery's founding "after 371" only in the editorial introduction). His death in 397 is the horizon's own fixed point. Whether Sulpitius's virtus-organized Life is modelled on the Vita Antonii (Stancliffe, row 18, unread) is open and bears on how much of G6 is the north's own literary form, not on any fact about Martin.

Two voices, both nodes. The rule of the cell (not leaving it, alone or with one other) is Cassian's Egyptian prescription, and whether any Gallic house kept it is not documented. The Latin cella / cellulis reaches us only through the editor's Introduction, in a sentence that is Cardinal Noris's (general reference only), not our own Latin as read.

The wording is Documented as Sulpitius's own text (Vita ch. XXIV, read at its locus for this record). The event is a Tier-3-shaped wonder - the devil appearing as Christ in Martin's cell - told by an author who was not present and who says he had it "from the lips of Martin himself"; Roberts's endnote 40 at the same locus records the editor's own doubt about the narrative. What this record carries as load-bearing is the formation ideal the words state (the Christ this world would own is the one who suffered), not the event; the words are Martin's as the tradition of Tours attributed them to him, never independently corroborated.

voice_event.text:
He went up on the cross for the salvation of the whole world and took away the debt that could not be paid. At the sixth hour, as the houses of Palestine and Mesopotamia handed it to us, the spotless Sacrifice, our Lord and Saviour, was offered up to the Father. Dead in the flesh, he was not dead in the spirit; his soul was not left in hell. He went down into hell at the ninth hour and brought out the captive saints. No one took his life from him; he laid it down himself and took it again.

And he came to us in the poor. A beggar stood at a city gate with no clothes, and everyone passed. A soldier cut his one cloak in two for him. That night the soldier saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. Among the brethren at Marseilles an elder of Egypt taught the same meeting.

What we held of his approach is this: he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation.

results.message: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text:
Humility. It was the root from which discretion and patience grew, and the only ground on which power might be held. Cassian gives it ten checkable signs - a monk could test himself against them. A count's son won "the true nobility" by hawking baskets. At Tours it was "the same humility in his heart" that Martin kept from his cell, sitting on a "rude little stool, such as those in use by the lowest of servants".

It was set above miracles. An elder of Egypt taught that we ought to refresh Christ in guests. Humility was what made that act right, not any power shown afterward.

The word came to us from Egypt's fathers through Cassian, and from Martin's own cell through Sulpitius. Both houses held it the same way, though they never wrote of each other.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, discretion is the virtue by which every other is kept from destroying itself. It is "the mother of all virtues, as well as their guardian and regulator," the "eye and light of the body," the "royal road" between excess and slackness. It is gained "only ... by true humility." glosses.quick_meaning: The virtue that keeps every other virtue from ruining itself. The royal road between excess and slackness, gained only by showing one's thoughts to the elders.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Discretion - you mean tact, or knowing when to keep quiet?' - no: the regulator of all the virtues, awarded that title by a council of Egyptian fathers, whose whole substance is the elders' judgment received through humility and disclosure, a money-changer's test of every thought on a royal road where "extremes meet" - a gift of grace, not a temperament.

discernment as a private spiritual intuition or a decision-making technique

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: We believed it because we saw it. A soldier at a city gate saw a beggar everyone else passed, and cut his one cloak in two for him. That night he saw Christ wearing the half he had given away. The Lord showed himself in the beggar's half of a soldier's cloak. Among the brethren at Marseilles an elder of Egypt taught it as what the fathers handed down. We received it from the fathers, not as a thing invented. The soldier at the gate was Martin himself. The disciples who came to Marmoutier were disciplined after the example of the saintly master. What he did at the gate was the thing they watched and copied. We believed it because it was received from antiquity, and because the man who handed it to us had done it.

glosses.plain_meaning: How formation passed from one person to another among us. A disciple was made by watching - and, later, by reading - a named man whose life was held up to copy. Our books were written to be that example when the man himself was absent.
glosses.quick_meaning: Formation by copying a named man, seen or read. Every one of our houses worked this way. It is why we wrote Lives, and why Cassian set down what the elders taught.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Aren't these Lives just legend, and "imitation" just copying?' - for us the Life was written by a man who says he saw, as the thing to be copied in deed and body, and imitation of a named master was the method by which every monk and bishop we produced was made; our literature is Lives and reported conferences rather than treatises for exactly this reason.

results.message: Tell me about someone who lived this out.

voice_event.speaker: gallic
voice_event.text: Vincent of Lérins lived it out. He dwelt on the island in the seclusion of a monastery and wrote a remembrancer against his own forgetting. He signed it "Peregrinus, the least of all the servants of God" - a teller, not an author. What he set down was the rule for telling the truth of Catholic faith from the falsehood of heretical pravity: hold that faith which has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When a part, a novelty, or a few dissent, prefer the whole, antiquity, and consent. He read the letter from the Apostolic See the same way. He called the faith a deposit - gold received, gold to be given back. He never told his own story of coming to believe, only that he left the storms of worldly warfare and cast anchor in the harbour of religion.

glosses.plain_meaning: A monastery, for us, is simply the place where monks dwell. Martin's wooden cell and the caves around it; a bishop's "new monastery" in a province without one; a house "for women" at Marseilles. Coenobium, the word Cassian brings from Egypt, names not the place but the kind of life kept in it. A congregation "governed by the direction of a single Elder."
glosses.quick_meaning: Simply where monks dwell - a wooden cell and caves, or a bishop's new house. The coenobium is the life kept there: one Elder over a congregation.
glosses.translational_sense: 'You mean an abbey - walls, a church, an abbot, a Rule?' - no: for us "monastery" meant nothing more than "the habitation of monks," a wooden hut and hollowed caves or a bishop's new foundation, and since even the false monks had "monasteries," the south reached for coenobium - one elder over a congregation - when it wanted to say what mattered.

glosses.plain_meaning: We gave the title "Pope" to bishops we revered. Cassian wrote to Pope Castor of Apta Julia. "The Apostolic See" was Vincent's word for Rome. It was first in authority and first in refusing anything new. The two words meant different things.

confidence.divergence_note: Documented as an author and a date: the Commonitory dates itself three years after the Council of Ephesus, to 434 (Doc_01 §2.3), and Gennadius ch. LXV (ancient text) records the work, the pseudonym, and the theft of "the greater part of the second book." Widely Accepted for the attribution to Vincentius. Contested whether he held or only sympathized with the Massilian position (Doc_02 §1); whether "Peregrinus" conceals anything is not settled by any Native text. His death is placed "before 450, and probably shortly after 434" on Gennadius's regnal formula (Doc_01 §2.4); his entry to Lerins is undated - "c. 425" is Inferential-Thin, a floating convention (Doc_01 §2.3) - and the claim that he was brother to Lupus of Troyes is Inferential-Thin and uncorroborated by Gennadius. Of the island he says only that he dwells "in the seclusion of a Monastery." Salvian (row 43) is not licensed for grace-related material and is not drawn on for him.

The word itself is the best-shared place-term in the lexicon (Sulpitius, Cassian, Salvian, Gennadius; both nodes). The coenobium / monastery distinction and the three kinds are single-voice (Cassian) and, by his own framing, Piamun's Egyptian teaching received. Two women's houses are attested (Tours, Marseilles) with no woman's voice from either. Lerins's internal layout is the least-documented house and is not described.

Contested-Tradition term, two contest types. Historical scope: whether the rule was ever applied as broadly or uniformly as its later use claims, and whether Vincent applied it consistently - Heurtley's Appendix III (editorial, unread) on Vincent's handling of Celestine's letter is the in-file instance, and the same rule that guarded the Massilian position was later turned against it (post-window). Relationship to present-day traditions: the "Vincentian canon" in Anglican, Roman Catholic and Orthodox argument; Heurtley's footnote at ch. 17 [44] quotes Newman (about Origen), not Vincent's own progress passage. Single-voice (Vincent) as a formulated rule of faith; Cassian's Inst. I.2 states the same three-part test for monastic custom, and Martin applies its instinct to a cult - parallels, not attestations of the formula. Vincent's own Latin for "rule" is not given in the vendored translation.

No Author Gravity as a word - all three founding voices, both nodes (Vincent's faith, Cassian's "approved Catholic fathers" and "Catholic rule" of custom, Sulpitius's party name against the Priscillianists). The definition - "comprehends all universally"; "everywhere, always, by all" - is Vincent's alone. "Roman Catholic" is a modern-hearing gap carried as distortion risk, not as a recorded live contest (Doc_06 section 3; no CT tag). No Latin lemma sought; Vincent's own Latin for "rule" is not given in the vendored translation.

Cross-voice in referent - three voices, three referents: Sulpitius's predicate of Martin (the apostles' power and standing, "deemed powerful and truly apostolical"), Cassian's summit of love and origin of the coenobium, Vincent's See. The referents never argue because they never meet. The northern predicate is single-voice (Sulpitius), and its historicity falls under virtus / power's Reported-Experience Status. Nobody in the south calls a living man "apostolical." No Latin lemma sought.

voice_event.text: That we never settled the question our whole life turned on. At Marseilles two friends came back to morning prayer troubled by one sentence an old man had added the night before: no one masters the good by his own toil. The elder cut the office short and answered with a farmer who still needs the rain. Which one began the good, grace or the will, we left open. The power that "always remains free in man" to "neglect or delight in the grace of God" was real enough that a monk's fasting, watching and labour were truly his and truly required. It was weak enough that "the assistance and grace of God are necessary to it every day and hour". A hostile outsider called the monks and clergy of Marseilles who held this Massilians. We never called ourselves that. We stopped where the fathers stopped.

glosses.plain_meaning: In Cassian's Marseilles, the help of God without which no effort reaches its goal. Grace "always co-operates with our will," and "assists, protects, and defends it." glosses.translational_sense: 'So were you on the side of grace or of works - were you semi-Pelagians?' - the label is a sixteenth-century coinage that appears in our own texts only in the editors' notes; what we held was help that co-operates and requires labour, on both sides at once, declared beyond reason's grasp - and a Representative who resolves it either way has left us.

confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted at the narrative level: Cassian's own first-person account - "when after a short sleep we returned for morning service ... Abbot Germanus was troubled" - in a work whose authorship and dating "not later than" 426 are Widely Accepted (Doc_01 §2.3); the literary-dialogue caveat is carried (the extended speeches are Cassian's composition of what he heard, decades later). Contested [CT] for what the Conference that grew from the question meant in relation to Augustine (Chadwick vs. Casiday, Doc_01 §7; gallic.term.grace, gallic.term.free-will), which this story neither depends on nor resolves - it records the question as Cassian says it arose, which Doc_05 §7.3 finds "compatible with both readings." The "previous discussion" the scruple arose from is Conference XII, On Chastity, which the vendored edition marks "Not translated" (Registry row 11): the story's own occasion is known here only from this chapter's summary of it. Gibson's headnote "On the Semi-Pelagianism of this Conference" is editorial and not the story's source. Registry row 9's C rating for content explicitly excepts Conf. XIII; XIII.1-3, 13, 18 read directly at Doc_09 (npnf211 divs iv.v.iv.i-iii).

confidence.divergence_note: Contested-Tradition term, two contest types. Meaning: whether Cassian's "co-operates," "precedes" and "inspires us with a good will to begin with" amount to Augustine's prevenient grace or to the position Prosper's Contra Collatorem attacked - the Chadwick (redating Honoratus so that Conf. XIII answers Augustine) versus Casiday (rejecting the redating; little direct polemic) contest, bound to the contested chronology; Cassian's own text says the beginning comes from God in some places and can arise "from our own efforts" in others (XIII.8, XIII.12). Application: whether "semi-Pelagian," a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus, fairly describes the Massilian position, and whether Vincent and Lerins held it at all (Heurtley's editorial claim, contested). Cross-voice: our own voice (Cassian), the provoking outsider reporting us (Augustine), and a later insider (Faustus, via Gennadius) do not speak in unison. Tours is silent because its corpus closed before the question was posed - an absence, not a disagreement. Faustus's own De gratia is unread beyond a bounded grep, so the in-window Lerins side cannot be stated in its own words.

Neither "Massilians" nor "semi-Pelagian" is any of our own voices' word. "Massilians" is a period-contemporary but hostile outsider's Marseilles-specific label (Prosper's, on Doc_01 section 7's grounds; the vendored file corroborates the usage only in Warfield's editorial note and in Augustine's chapter heading), used by this build as shorthand for a position also held at Lerins. "Semi-Pelagian" is a sixteenth-century coinage present in our files only in the editors' apparatus and is not a candidate. CT tag (Application to this world): the contest is whether the label applies to our own voices at all - it names one city, from outside, for a stance our own texts never label. The Representative does not use either word of itself.
